job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Omar Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior adviser's assistant at a mortgage broker in Sheffield. Basically, I gather the paperwork for first-time buyers, run the affordability numbers and write the case summary for the adviser, Dev. I use an AI assistant for most of the drafting and I've built my own checklist for missing documents. I pray at the mosque on Fridays, then spend the weekend on my side project. I rent a room in a house with two other guys, and I've got a heavy student loan and almost nothing in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not magic, but it's a good tool for people who do the work. At the mosque I'd say hard work and honest dealing still matter more than any machine. Online I'd post that people complain about AI and then use it five times a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm okay about the plateau, because the tools I use already give me an edge. My worry is money. I've got a big loan, my room costs a lot, and nobody in my family has any spare to help. The market for finance jobs is small around here, so I'd have to hold onto this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools at work and look for more ways to be useful to Dev. I'd put 100 a month into the loan. At the weekends I'd carry on with my side project and try to get my first five paying clients by spring. I'd also keep my Friday routine, because it keeps my head straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, honestly, with a nagging bit about money. I've got a good engine and a very small fuel tank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the side project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm building a simple bookkeeping service for corner shops and halal butchers near us. I use an AI assistant to sort their receipts and make their VAT summary, and I charge a fixed 60 a month. I have two customers so far, my uncle's shop and a barber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the broker feel about the tools you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev likes it, because I get through the case notes in half the time. My manager, Sandra, is more careful, she asks me to double-check everything. That's fair. I tell her what the tool did and what I did, so nobody feels tricked.

say: I'd say it's not magic but a good tool for people who do the **work**.
Online I'd say people **complain** about AI and then use it five times a day.
think: The tools I use already give me an **edge**, so the plateau doesn't worry me.
My worry is **money**: a big loan, an expensive room and no family spare.
do: Look for more ways to be **useful** to Dev with the tools.
Put **100** a month into the loan.
Get my first five paying **clients** for the side project by spring.
feel: **Confident**, with a nagging worry: a good engine and a very small fuel tank.
S0.quote: I've got a good engine and a very small fuel tank.
fieldNote: He sees AI as an **advantage**; the loan is his only real fear.
His side project is already earning from two customers.
He's open with his manager about what the tool did, to keep trust.

steps.text: Use AI to speed up case summaries for Dev
Put 100 a month toward the student loan
Sign five paying shop clients for my bookkeeping service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity, and the people who'll do well are the ones who learn to work with it early. I'd say governments shouldn't get in the way but should help people retrain. I'd say work is a duty and a dignity, and that I want to keep being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm quite optimistic, but I know I might be wrong. My job is paperwork and numbers, so a lot of it can be done by software. If it's me plus a good assistant, I'd do the work of three. That helps me, but it could also mean the broker hires fewer assistants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn myself into the person at the broker who runs the AI side, so I'm the one who makes everyone else faster. I'd grow my bookkeeping service to 15 shops by the end of the year, with an AI doing most of the sorting. I'd also open a small savings account and put 200 a month in it, no excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a little bit hungry. It's like the first morning of Ramadan when you know what's ahead and you're ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your job be safe in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe if I'm the one who runs the tools, less safe if I'm just the one who types. Dev's clients still want a person to talk to, and I think I'd be in the room more. But if the broker consolidates, the first to go would be the assistants who've not learned the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family react to you building your own thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father runs a small grocery. My father says a man who works for himself eats his own harvest. He worries about my loan, and he doesn't understand the AI, but he likes the idea that I might own something. My mother just wants me to be home for Eid.

say: I'd say it's a big **opportunity** for people who learn to work with it early.
I'd say work is a **duty** and a dignity, and I want to keep being useful.
think: Paperwork and numbers are my job, so software can do **a lot** of it.
With a good assistant I'd do the work of three, which helps me but could mean **fewer hires**.
do: Become the broker's **AI person**, making everyone else faster.
Grow my bookkeeping service to **15 shops** by the end of the year.
Put **200** a month into a savings account, no excuses.
feel: **Excited** and hungry, like the first morning of Ramadan.

fieldNote: He wants to be the person who runs the **tools**, not the one replaced by them.
He credits family and faith for his drive, and his father's idea of ownership.
He is honest that his optimism could be wrong.

steps.text: Become the broker's go-to person for AI tools
Grow my bookkeeping service to 15 shops this year
Put 200 a month into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the world is about to change faster than politics can follow, and that we have to look after each other. At the mosque I'd say let's help the families who'll be hit hardest. At work I'd say the broker needs to decide what a human adds. And I'd say it before somebody else decided it for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a lot more worried. If AI does almost all thinking work better and cheaper, a mortgage broker's assistant is among the first to go. And my side project, bookkeeping for shops, is also thinking work. Everything I'm building could be copied by the machines in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost I can and try to get 3000 in the bank, since I'd need a safety net, and then I'd look for something the machines can't copy easily: owning a physical shop, running a business with a real storefront, or being a partner in my uncle's grocery. I'd also look for any chance to buy a share of something, rather than only earn a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buzzing, but in a nervous way. It's like standing at the starting line of a race where everybody runs faster than you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight. My father would say we've been through harder times, which is true, and he'd offer a room above the shop. I'd say thank you and mean it, but I wouldn't take it unless I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change what you'd tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every day into the bookkeeping side to see if it could work as a stand-alone business, and I'd look for an angle that a machine can't do alone, like handling people's tax letters in person, in their own language. In my community that matters. People trust a face they know.

say: I'd say the world will change faster than **politics** can follow, so we must look after each other.
At the mosque I'd say let's help the families who'll be **hit hardest**.
think: A broker's assistant is among the **first to go**, and my bookkeeping side project is thinking work too.

S2.quote: People trust a face they know.
fieldNote: His **ownership** instinct sharpens: a share in the grocery or his own shop.

He expects his own side business could be copied, and is honest about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good amount of time to get ready, and I'd tell people to start now. I'd say the fastest learners will have an advantage and that we should share what we learn with those who are slower. That's the community way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd see it as my best shot. By 2031 I could have a decent business with real customers, a loan half gone and some equity in a shop. The risk is that I'm too cocky and I put all my effort into the one idea. I've seen young guys do that and end up with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the bookkeeping service into a small firm with a few part-time helpers and a proper office. I'd aim for 40 clients and 2000 a month profit by the end of year three. I'd pay the loan down by 250 a month. And I'd keep a day job as long as it's there, since a salary pays for the experiments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit prayerful about it. I think I can do something real with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What difference do five years make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a trusted local finance service for shops, taxi drivers and families, bookkeeping and tax and mortgage advice, with AI doing the heavy lifting and me doing the talking. The mortgage side is my job now, so I'd know it well. The community would be the moat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't put it all into one thing. I'll keep a second plan: a qualification in financial advice, which regulators will still want a human to hold. It's boring but it's insurance. I'd rather have a boring licence and a clever idea than just one of them.

I'd say the fastest learners should **share** what they learn with the slower ones.

fieldNote: Five years gives him a **business** plan with numbers and a hedge: a licence.

steps.text: Grow the bookkeeping service into a small firm with helpers
Study for a financial advice qualification
Pay down the loan by 250 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a gift, and that we shouldn't waste it. I'd say people should start small businesses, learn the tools and teach their children, and that community groups should run classes. I'd say the future will go to the people who plan, not the people who wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pretty calm. By 2036 I'd be 32, married, with a business or two and the loan long gone. Even if AGI takes a lot of thinking work, I'd have owned things that make money without me. My risk is thinking I've got all the time in the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my firm, buy a small flat as an investment, and pay the loan off in five or six years. I'd also put a regular amount into a low-cost fund and help my parents with the shop's online side. And I'd do an evening course in financial advice, so I have a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. It feels like planting a tree and knowing I'll sit under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What does success look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house, a wife I love, kids who see me at dinner, a business that runs without me every minute, and helping my parents rest. I don't need to be rich. I'd want to be useful and not worried about the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the danger of too much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Complacency. I'd put a note in my phone to review everything every Ramadan, as a yearly reset: what's working, what's not, who needs help. It's a good habit for the soul as well as the business.

say: I'd say it's a **gift** and we shouldn't waste it.
I'd say the future goes to the people who **plan**, not the ones who wait.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 with a business or two and the **loan gone**.
My risk is thinking I've got all the **time** in the world.

S4.quote: The future will go to the people who plan, not the people who wait.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **calm**, with owned assets as his shield.

steps.text: Build my bookkeeping firm and clear the loan in six years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I move fast, but two years isn't enough to own anything solid, and everything I do is thinking work. What would help is cheap capital for young people starting small, community networks that share what works, and a regulator that keeps a human in the loop for advice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people say my generation wants handouts. I want a fair shot and a bit of capital. Give me that and I'll build something that employs other people.

headlineQuote: I want a fair shot and a bit of capital. Give me that and I'll build something that employs other people.
portrait: Omar is a **22-year-old** mortgage broker's assistant in Sheffield, with a heavy loan, almost no savings and no family money.
He's traditional and free-market, rooted in his mosque and family, and sure that work and ownership give dignity.
He uses AI every day and runs a small bookkeeping service for corner shops and halal butchers on the side.
He's uneasy in most worlds, anxious when AGI arrives in two years, and calm with ten years to build.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because it's too short to own anything solid and his work is thinking work.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap capital** for young people starting small, community networks that share what works, and a human kept in the loop for advice.
